$comment: The values this repository is willing to pass for arguments the inventory cannot give a
domain to, plus the arguments it refuses to vary and why.
Paths point inside the oracle container, where MakeFixtures.java writes the corpus. They are
not committed files: the corpus is rebuilt from the program on every run, which keeps it
deterministic and keeps binary fixtures out of the tree.
Adding a value here widens a covering array. Adding an exclusion narrows it, and the reason
is required, because an exclusion is the one thing in this file that can hide a difference.
There is no constraint forbidding a block-compressed input with a `.idx` output. The reference
REFUSES that pair by name, and a refusal is behaviour a port has to reproduce, so the row is
kept and both sides are compared on the refusal rather than on an output.
`--bgzf-file` takes a block-compressed file and a plain one: the second is a refusal the
reference makes by name, and a row that reproduces a refusal is as much of the claim as a row
that reproduces a report.
`--input` carries the BAM as well as the three feature files: it is one argument name on two
kinds of tool, and a read walker refuses a VCF the way IndexFeatureFile refuses a BAM, so both
refusals are rows rather than exclusions.
`--variant` takes an INDEXED VCF and an unindexed one. A feature walker refuses `-L` against
an input with no random access, so a list with only the unindexed file would compare two
refusals on every interval row and never reach a traversal; and dropping the unindexed one
would lose that refusal, which is behaviour too.
`CountVariants` overrides `--output`: the shared list is an index's name, and this tool writes
a count. A `.idx` there would measure nothing but a file name.
`--use-jdk-deflater` used to be excluded here, on the ground that these tools write nothing
compressed. That stopped being true when IndexFeatureFile learned to write a tabix index: a
.tbi is a BGZF file, and the deflater decides its bytes. The argument is a boolean with a
domain of its own, so it needs no fixture; what it needed was for the exclusion to be read
again after the tool changed.
`--reference` takes two FASTAs, each with the .fai and .dict beside it that GATK requires: one
on the corpus's own contig and one on a contig it does not carry. The reference dictionary
takes part in the validation and outranks the reads' in the best-available chain, so the
second value is a refusal and the first is not.
`GatherVcfsCloud` holds `--create-output-variant-index` at FALSE, and the reason is the
measurement rather than the port. A Tribble index records the last-modified time of the file
it indexes, and here that file is the tool's own OUTPUT: the two sides write their own copy at
their own moment, so the two indexes differ in eight bytes of clock and the row measures when
the run happened. The port builds the index byte for byte otherwise -- checked against the
reference's own on one input -- and every other tool indexes a file both sides were GIVEN.
`--read-index` takes two paths that both exist, because what the argument decides is not
whether the file is there: an index handed to an input that is neither a BAM nor a CRAM is
refused by htsjdk's text-SAM branch whatever it contains, and the count is checked against the
number of reads inputs before the contents are read at all.
`--sequence-dictionary` takes two: one that agrees with the corpus's contig and one that
shares nothing with it. The MASTER dictionary is validated against every other one before the
traversal, so the second value is a refusal and the first is not, and both are behaviour.
Four arguments are here with a SECOND value and no expectation that they change anything:
`--tmp-dir`, the two cloud prefetch buffers and `--seconds-between-progress-updates`. Each was
excluded as having one value, which meant the array covered it by holding it at its default
and could not have noticed if it mattered. A row that varies them and gets the same answer on
both sides is a claim; a row that never varied them was not.
`--exclude-intervals` and the two paddings are here because the four arguments beside `-L` in
IntervalArgumentCollection had no domain at all: an int with only its default is excluded as
having one value, and a free-form string with no default is excluded for having none. With no
values they were covered by being absent, which is the one setting that cannot disagree.
The three read-filter arguments are here for the same reason. `--inverted-read-filter` names
filters that are neither a tool default nor a value of `--read-filter`: inverting a default is
refused outright, and inverting a filter the same row enables is refused too, so an overlap
would spend rows on refusals the unit suite already covers. And
`--disable-read-filter` names WellformedReadFilter, which IS the default, so the row actually
removes a filter rather than warning about one that was never there. Both take a second value
because one is no domain at all: an argument with a single value is covered by being present
or absent, which the generator excludes for the same reason it excludes a lone default.
$per_tool: A tool whose `--INPUT` is not the kind of file the shared value names declares its own here,
as `"per_tool": { "<Tool>": { "--INPUT": [...] } }`. The override replaces the shared list
`CreateHadoopBamSplittingIndex` declares its own `--input` and `--output`: the shared input
list carries three feature files this tool refuses by EXTENSION before it opens anything, so
an array built from it would measure one refusal four times. Two values are enough to have the
refusal and the index both.
It takes TWO names for the same reason every other argument here does: one value is covered by
being present or absent, and the second is what lets a row notice that the tool writes where it
was told to.
for that tool only. This repository has no such tool yet; picard-rs does, and the mechanism
lives here because the generator does.
See tools/coverage/README.md.
`reads2.bam` is the second BAM, and the reason it exists is that an argument with ONE fixture
value is held at it: the row carries it, no row varies it, and nothing can notice whether it
matters. Every read-taking tool therefore names two BAMs. They differ in the three ways the
corpus needs: a different record count, positions on the other side of both interval fixtures,
and two records the default read filters disagree about (a leading-deletion cigar that
`GoodCigarReadFilter` refuses, and an unmapped record that `MappedReadFilter` removes).
`recal2.table` and `reads2.bai` follow it, so `--bqsr-recal-file` and `--read-index` have a
value that belongs to the input in the row and a value that belongs to the other one.
The read tools name their own `--intervals` as well, and the reason is `distinct_outputs`
rather than acceptance: the shared `chr1:1-1000` holds two of the first BAM's reads and the
exclusion fixture removes one of them, so every accepted row answered 0 or 1 and an array of
twenty rows observed two outputs. `chr1:1-6000` spans all eight reads of `reads.bam` and three
of `reads2.bam`, and `chr1:50000-60000` spans none of the first and two of the second, which is
what makes a padding, an exclusion or a read filter visible as a different number.
`CountVariants` names its own `--input` for a reason the other tools do not have: it is a
VARIANT walker, so `--input` is the optional READS beside the driving variants, and the shared
list carries three feature files. A row that pairs one of those with a `--read-index` is
refused by htsjdk before the tool runs (`Cannot use index file with textual SAM file`), which
was fourteen of its thirty-one rows measuring one refusal. Two BAMs and the indexes that belong
to them turn those rows into traversals whose reads dictionary is compared against the
features', which is what the tool actually does with them.
`CountBases` and `FlagStat` take `CountReads`' values verbatim, which is the archetype paying
for itself: the three declare the same seventy arguments and read the same files, so the
fixtures that made one measurable make all three.
`CountBasesInReference` names the two BAMs even though a reference walker never opens them:
the standard read arguments are its inheritance, so a row pairing a `--read-index` with the
shared list's feature files is refused by htsjdk before the tool runs, and eleven of its
twenty-three rows measured that one refusal. It names the read walkers' intervals for the
same reason the others do: the corpus's reference carries the same contig.
`SplitIntervals` writes a DIRECTORY, so its `--output` values are two directory names the run
creates rather than two files. Its own five arguments carry two values each: a scatter count
of one and of three, a minimum contig size that keeps both contigs and one that drops the
second, and the two halves of a file name.
`--interval-file-prefix` carries two NON-EMPTY names, and the tool's own default is the empty
string: a covering array writes every argument as `--name value`, so an empty value leaves the
next token to be read as a positional argument and the row is refused before the tool runs.
`Pileup` takes the read walkers' corpus because it IS a read walker's startup with a different
traversal after it. `PreprocessIntervals` opens no reads and still DECLARES them, so it takes
the two BAMs for the same reason `CountBasesInReference` does: a row pairing a `--read-index`
with the shared list's feature files is refused by htsjdk before the tool runs. Its own two
arguments, `--bin-length` and `--padding`, are what decide the bins it writes.
`IllegalArgumentException`s: the merging rule must be OVERLAPPING_ONLY and the interval padding
must be zero, because the tool bins and pads by its own `--bin-length` and `--padding` instead.
Each is held at the one value the tool accepts; varying them measured that refusal on nine of
twenty-one rows and nothing else.
`PreprocessIntervals` refuses FOUR of the standard interval arguments in its own
`IllegalArgumentException`s -- the set rule must be UNION, the exclusion padding and the
interval padding must be zero, and the merging rule must be OVERLAPPING_ONLY -- because it bins
reproduces each refusal, so a row that carries one measures behaviour rather than a gap.
and each is HELD at the value the tool accepts. Varying them measured the refusal on twenty of
twenty-one rows and left ONE distinct output, which is an array that covers its arguments
without testing them; held, the same array runs nine accepted rows over four outputs. The
refusals are the runner's and are reproduced -- they are simply not what these rows spend
themselves on.
`PrintDistantMates` and `GetSampleName` take the read walkers' corpus unchanged, which is what
the archetype is for: the first writes a BAM like `PrintReads` and the second reads a header
and nothing else, and both open the same files by the same arguments.
`PrintDistantMates` names `pairs.bam` first, and it is the only tool that needs it: every
record's mate is read, and the other BAMs are unpaired, so the REFERENCE answered `Cannot get
mate information for an unpaired read` on eight of its rows. The second value is one of those
unpaired BAMs, which keeps that refusal in the array rather than losing it.
`CompareIntervalLists` names `--L` and `--L2`, which are ITS OWN scalars rather than the
engine's interval collection: two values each, so the array sees the same list compared with
itself and a shorter one compared with a longer, which are the three verdicts the tool has.
`CompareIntervalLists` writes NO FILE: its verdict is a line on standard output or an
exception, and the corpus records the output files plus the first error line. So its accepted
rows all read as the empty output and `distinct_outputs` is 1 by construction rather than for
want of fixtures -- what the array measures for this tool is which of the three verdicts each
row reaches, and two of them are exceptions the corpus does record.
`AnnotateIntervals` holds the same four interval arguments `PreprocessIntervals` holds, and for
the same reason: both call `validateIntervalArgumentCollection`, and varying them measures that
refusal instead of the table the tool writes.
`CheckPileup` takes `Pileup`'s corpus -- one locus walker's startup is the other's -- plus the
two mpileup files it compares against: `truth.pileup` is the REFERENCE's own `Pileup` output
converted to samtools' six columns, so it agrees with the traversal at every locus, and
`wrong.pileup` disagrees at the first, which is the difference between a run that validates and
a run that is refused.
It HOLDS `--max-depth-per-sample` at zero, which is the one hold in this file that names a gap
in the port rather than a refusal in the tool: any value above zero asks for the locus
iterator's leveling downsampler, which the port does not carry, so the row would compare a
traversal against the port's own limitation message. `Pileup` varies the same argument and
measures nothing by it -- every one of its rows carrying two is refused earlier, for a
dictionary the reads do not match -- so the argument has never actually been measured here.
gatk-rs#1102 is the downsampler; when it lands both tools can vary this again.
`FastaReferenceMaker` takes `CountBasesInReference`'s corpus, which is the reference walker's:
the reads it declares are never opened and are there so that a `--read-index` paired with a
feature file is refused by htsjdk rather than measured. Its own `--line-width` carries the
writer's default and a width narrow enough to wrap the corpus's intervals more than once, which
is what makes the argument visible in the FASTA rather than only present.
`CollectReadCounts` HOLDS `--format` at TSV, and that is the second hold naming a gap in the
port rather than a refusal in the tool: the tool's own default is HDF5, which is a file format
this port does not write at all (gatk-rs#1107). It holds the same four interval arguments
`PreprocessIntervals` and `AnnotateIntervals` hold, for the same reason and by the same
`validateIntervalArgumentCollection`.

exclude.--help: prints the usage and returns; the row would measure the argument parser rather than the tool
exclude.--version: prints the version and returns, same reason
exclude.--QUIET: suppresses the log on stderr, and what is compared is stdout and the output file
exclude.--verbosity: log level on stderr, same reason
exclude.--use-jdk-inflater: chooses an inflater, and the input is read the same way either way
exclude.--gcs-max-retries: reaches nothing without a cloud path in the row
exclude.--gcs-project-for-requester-pays: reaches nothing without a cloud path in the row
exclude.--gatk-config-file: a configuration file the corpus does not carry; varying it would measure the config loader
exclude.--arguments_file: expands into the command line itself, which is measured by the barclay-arguments-file suite instead
exclude.--quantize-quals: mutually exclusive with BOTH static-quantized-quals and round-down-quantized, and a covering array assigns every argument in every row: Barclay's mutex fires on an argument being SET, so even --round-down-quantized false refuses the row. Holding this one at its default is what lets the other two be varied, which is two covered arguments rather than one. The mutex message is measured by the mutex-target-names suite
exclude.--metadata: a feature source the Pileup runner does not open: it refuses the argument rather than answering without the column it asks for, so a row carrying one would measure the refusal
exclude.--mappability-track: a feature file the AnnotateIntervals runner does not open: it refuses the argument rather than writing a table without the column it asks for, so a row carrying one measures the refusal
exclude.--segmental-duplication-track: a feature file the AnnotateIntervals runner does not open: it refuses the argument rather than writing a table without the column it asks for, so a row carrying one measures the refusal
